proposed_edges.relationship: Smout’s ‘The Highlands and the Roots of Green Consciousness’ (1991; lecture 1990) invokes Keith Thomas’s Man and the Natural World (1983) for the eighteenth-century change in educated attitudes to nature.
proposed_edges.map_label: Thomas on changing attitudes to nature
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh OCR reading of the official British Academy scan, printed pp. 238–239 and n. 8. Smout explicitly credits ‘Keith Thomas in particular’ for describing this change; n. 8 identifies the 1983 book. The surrounding argument distinguishes earlier Scottish appreciation of nature from the later changes among educated outsiders. This is a named intellectual resource, not a claim that Thomas originated Scottish environmental awareness. Thomas’s book itself unread; the lecture was delivered in 1990 and published in 1991.

proposed_edges.relationship: Smout and Devine were the founding editors of Scottish Economic and Social History, first published in 1981.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Devine’s institutional CV, printed p. 3, section (d), item 6, states ‘founding editor with T.C. Smout’; it distinguishes the planning committee of 1979 and Devine’s tenure ending in 1984. Scott Hames’s chapter (online 2025; print 2026), section ‘Writing about Scotland Became Itself a Form of Nationalism’, first paragraph, independently dates their joint founding of the journal to 1981. These selected passages were read. No claim that Smout’s tenure also ended in 1984, no supervision claim, and no shared political position inferred. First-issue editorial and subsequent journal contents unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Keith Thomas reads it in ‘The Long March’ (1984), Smout’s ‘Scotland and England’ (1980) supplies an industrializing Scottish counterexample to the core–periphery account associated with Wallerstein and Braudel.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated evidence: Thomas’s 1984 review, passage beginning ‘Even more debatable’ through the paragraph beginning ‘In recent years’, plus n. 7. He names Wallerstein, explains the core–periphery claim, then cites Smout for primary producers escaping the industrialization trap. Smout’s Review 3:4 (1980), pp. 601–630, is unread; those pages are citation metadata, not pages consulted. Thomas reviews Braudel and distinguishes the two theorists. No wholesale rejection of world-systems analysis or account of Wallerstein’s reply is proposed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Smout’s ‘Land and Sea: The Environment’ (2012) cites McNeill’s Something New Under the Sun (2000) for Glasgow’s coal-smoke pollution and its burden on human health.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Authorized preview, printed p. 29, first paragraph and n. 29, freshly read. Smout quotes ‘experienced newspaper editors left extra space for obituaries during smog sieges’ and gives Glasgow mortality and soot figures; n. 29 explicitly cites McNeill (2000), pp. 63, 66, 70–71. Those are Smout’s references, not pages independently read here. McNeill’s book and quantitative estimates remain unverified. A specific evidential use, not adoption of McNeill’s entire framework.
